This companion reproduces the chapter's financial calculations in Python.
The dataset and frozen split manifest are supplied in the repository.
The manifest preserves R's training/test membership and row order. A seed
alone would produce a different split in NumPy. R is not needed at runtime.

Statsmodels fits unpenalized binomial GLMs, with the same treatment contrasts
as R. Quantiles use linear interpolation, corresponding to R's default type 7.
Density curves use SciPy's KDE bandwidth, so their smoothing differs slightly
from R's plotting defaults. Numbered results retain the book's identifiers.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.api as sm
from scipy.special import expit
from scipy.stats import norm
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter, StrMethodFormatter
from IPython.display import display
from shared.output import setup,show_table,show_figure,finish,BLUE,RED,GREEN
from shared.scoring import load_data,design,policy,strategy,calibration,metrics,classification,cases,display_frame
from shared.scoring_figures import distributions,boxes,density,roc_plot,calibration_plot,COLORS
out = setup('01-logistic')
raw,income_ok,clean,train,test,original_names = load_data()
```

## 1.2 Data exploration and cleaning

The recorded default label is `loan_status`, renamed `loan_st` for analysis, with 1 for default and 0 for no default. The supplied documentation leaves its follow-up horizon unspecified. Throughout Chapters 1 and 2, a fitted PD estimates the probability of this label conditional on the model's inputs. Its interpretation as an annual or lifetime PD remains unvalidated and would require a documented observation horizon and outcome validation over that horizon.

The income plots below use stacked bin counts. Each dot represents one record;
their horizontal positions are income-bin centers rather than exact incomes.

```{python}
def income_dots(frame,width):
    bins = np.floor(frame.income.to_numpy()/width).astype(int)
    centers,counts = np.unique(bins,return_counts=True)
    fig,ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.scatter(np.repeat((centers+.5)*width,counts),
               np.concatenate([np.arange(n) for n in counts]),s=2,alpha=.35,color=BLUE)
    ax.set(xlabel='Annual income ($)',yticks=[],ylabel='')
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter('{x:,.0f}'))
    return fig
```

## 1.3 Fitting logistic models

The design helper constructs columns explicitly. It keeps the reference
category for each factor and applies natural logarithms to loan amount and
income. Its source is in `shared/scoring.py`.

```{python}
display(pd.DataFrame({'Sample':['Cleaned','Training','Test'],
                      'Records':[len(clean),len(train),len(test)],
                      'Default rate':[clean.loan_st.mean(),train.loan_st.mean(),test.loan_st.mean()]}))
models,pred = {},{}
for name in ['age','int','multi','full']:
    models[name] = sm.GLM(train.loan_st.to_numpy(float),design(train,name),
                          family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit(tol=1e-10,maxiter=100)
    pred[name] = np.asarray(models[name].predict(design(test,name)))
display(models['multi'].summary())
beta0,beta1 = models['age'].params
display(pd.DataFrame({'Age':[18,60],'Score':beta0+beta1*np.array([18,60]),
                      'Predicted PD':expit(beta0+beta1*np.array([18,60]))}))
```

### Figure 1.4 {#result-figure-1-4}
```{python}
ages = np.arange(-1000,501)
fig,ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.8))
ax.plot(ages,expit(beta0+beta1*ages),color=COLORS['age'])
for age,xytext in zip([train.age.min(),train.age.max()],[(.66,.42),(.83,.73)]):
    p = expit(beta0+beta1*age)
    ax.vlines(age,0,p,color=RED,ls=':',lw=.8)
    ax.hlines(p,ages.min(),age,color=RED,ls=':',lw=.8)
    ax.plot(age,p,'o',color=RED)
    ax.annotate(f'Age {age:.0f}\nPD {p:.2%}',(age,p),xytext=xytext,textcoords='axes fraction',
                arrowprops={'arrowstyle':'-','ls':':','color':RED},ha='center',
                bbox={'facecolor':'white','edgecolor':'none'})
ax.set(xlabel='Age',ylabel='Age-model predicted default probability')
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1))
show_figure(out,'1.4',fig)
```

```{python}
odds['Reading'] = np.where(odds['p-value']>=.05,'Unclear at 5%',
```

```{python}
def cutoff_density(cutoff):
    fig,ax = plt.subplots()
    grid,d = density(ax,full,'Full logistic',BLUE)
    ax.axvline(cutoff,color=RED,ls='--',lw=.9)
    ax.set_ylim(0,d.max()*1.4)
    for x,text in [(cutoff/2,f'Accepted\n{(full<=cutoff).mean():.1%}'),
                    (cutoff+.55*(full.max()-cutoff),f'Rejected\n{(full>cutoff).mean():.1%}')]:
        ax.text(x,d.max()*1.32,text,ha='center',va='top',
                bbox={'facecolor':'white','edgecolor':'none'})
    return fig
```

## 1.5 Confusion matrices and acceptance targets

```{python}
cm15 = classification(full,y,.15)
display(pd.Series(cm15))
cut80 = np.quantile(full,.8,method='linear')
cut65 = np.quantile(full,.65,method='linear')
print('80% target maps to PD cutoff:',cut80)
print('Realized acceptance:',np.mean(full<=cut80))
```

The target is a quantile input. The realized rate counts predictions at or
below the resulting cutoff, including ties. Linear interpolation locates a
cutoff between adjacent sorted scores; it does not smooth the score distribution.

The always-no-default rule accepts every applicant, including those who default, while the always-default rule rejects every applicant. The usefulness of these rules and the fitted-model cutoff depends on repayment and default payoffs and on the bank's lending capacity. Accuracy alone is insufficient to establish which policy is useful.

```{python}
fig,axes = plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(9,4),sharey=True)
for ax,k in zip(axes,['age','full']):
    b = bank[k]
    ax.plot(b.accept_rate,b.bad_rate,color=COLORS[k],lw=2)

        row = policy(pred[k],y,q)
        ax.vlines(q,0,row['bad_rate'],color=RED,ls=':',lw=.6)
        ax.hlines(row['bad_rate'],0,q,color=RED,ls=':',lw=.6)
    ax.set(title=k,xlabel='Target acceptance rate',xlim=(0,1),ylim=(0,max(y.mean()*1.25,.15)))
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1,decimals=1))
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1,decimals=0))
axes[0].set_ylabel('Bad rate among accepted loans')
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
best = payoff.loc[payoff.net_payoff.idxmax()]
show_table(out,'1.20',pd.DataFrame({'Quantity':['Target acceptance','Accepted good loans',
    'Good-loan payoff ($)','Accepted defaults','Default cost ($)','Net payoff ($)'],
    'Value':[best.accept_rate,best.accepted_good,best.accepted_good,best.accepted_defaults,
```

### Table 1.21 {#result-table-1-21}
```{python}
cost_rows = []
for cost in [2,5,10,15]:
    s = strategy(full,y,cost=cost)
    row = s.loc[s.net_payoff.idxmax()].to_dict()
    row['Default cost ($)'] = cost
    cost_rows.append(row)
show_table(out,'1.21',display_frame(pd.DataFrame(cost_rows)))
el_pd,el_ead,el_lgd = full[0],test.iloc[0].l_amnt,.6
el_expected_loss = el_pd*el_ead*el_lgd
display(pd.Series({'PD':el_pd,'EAD ($)':el_ead,'LGD':el_lgd,'Expected loss ($)':el_expected_loss}))
```

The preceding expected-loss calculation maps the first test applicant's fitted label probability into dollars using the original loan amount as EAD and an assumed LGD of 60%. Because the default label has an undocumented follow-up horizon, this is an illustrative monetary mapping under the assumption that PD, LGD, and EAD refer to the same exposure and horizon. Interpreting the result as annual expected loss would require documenting that horizon and validating the inputs for a one-year period.

The acceptance strategies use the observed test outcomes to illustrate financial
trade-offs. Selecting the best row here is a retrospective comparison. A lending
policy requires separate tuning and prospective validation.
